title: Estimation, Confidence Intervals and the Bootstrap
description: Point estimates and their uncertainty, confidence intervals from theory, and the bootstrap for statistics without a formula.
overview: An estimate without a statement of its uncertainty is half an answer. 'The conversion rate is 12.3%' means little until we know whether that could easily have been 10% or 15% with a different sample. A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for the parameter, and its width says how much the data can tell us.

For a mean or a proportion there are formulas for the interval, based on the central limit theorem. For most other statistics (a median, a ratio, a correlation, the AUC of a classifier) there are none that are simple. The bootstrap solves this with the computer: it resamples the data to simulate the sampling distribution. This chapter covers both, with the care needed to interpret the intervals correctly.
objectives: Compute a confidence interval for a mean (z and t) and a proportion, and interpret it correctly.
Explain what the confidence level means, and distinguish confidence, prediction and credible intervals.
Carry out the bootstrap for the standard error and percentile interval of any statistic.
Choose the sample size needed for a target interval width.
State when the bootstrap fails and how to use it in machine learning evaluation.

sections.title: Confidence intervals
terms: margin of error of a mean
body: A poll says 52% of voters support a measure, plus or minus 3 points. The 52% is the best single guess, and the plus or minus tells you how much that guess could be off because only a sample was asked. If another sample were drawn, it would give a slightly different number, and the interval is a way of saying how different. A wider interval means the data say less. A **point estimate** (x̄, p̂) is one number. A **confidence interval** (CI) adds a range. By the central limit theorem the sample mean is approximately normal around μ with standard deviation σ/√n (see Limit Theorems), so the probability that x̄ lies within 1.96 standard errors of μ is 95%. Turning this around, the interval x̄ ± 1.96 σ/√n contains μ in 95% of repeated samples.

The standard deviation σ is usually unknown and is replaced by the sample standard deviation s. This extra uncertainty makes the standardized statistic (x̄ − μ)/(s/√n) follow a **t distribution** with n − 1 **degrees of freedom**, which has heavier tails than the normal for small n. The interval is
where t* is the critical value of the t distribution (2.064 for 24 degrees of freedom and 95%; 1.96 in the limit of large n). For a proportion the Wald interval is p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).

example.title: A confidence interval for a mean
example.problem: From n = 25 customers the average basket is x̄ = 100 dollars with s = 15. Find the 95% interval for the true mean, and compare with the z interval.
example.solution: SE = 15/√25 = 3. With 24 degrees of freedom t* = 2.064, so the interval is 100 ± 2.064(3) = 100 ± 6.19 = (93.8, 106.2). The normal value 1.96 would give 100 ± 5.88, too narrow for such a small sample. With n = 100 the two would nearly agree.

example.title: A confidence interval for a proportion
example.problem: In 100 emails, 30 are flagged by a model. Find a 95% interval for the true flag rate.
example.solution: p̂ = 0.30 and SE = √(0.3 × 0.7/100) = 0.0458. The interval is 0.30 ± 1.96(0.0458) = 0.30 ± 0.090 = (0.21, 0.39). For small samples or p near 0 or 1, the Wald interval performs badly (it can extend below 0); the Wilson or exact (Clopper–Pearson) intervals are better.

body: The 95% refers to the **procedure**: if we repeated the study many times and built an interval each time, about 95% of the intervals would contain the true parameter. For any one computed interval, the parameter is either inside it or not. It is wrong to say 'there is a 95% probability that μ is in (93.8, 106.2)' in the frequentist reading, though many people do; a Bayesian **credible interval** (see Bayesian Methods) does have that meaning, given a prior.

list: A wider interval means less precision. Width is proportional to s/√n, so quadrupling n halves the width. A higher confidence level (99% instead of 95%) widens the interval.
Intervals assume a random sample (see Sampling and Experiments), independent observations, and, for small n, approximately normal data. They do not account for bias.

A **prediction interval** is for a //new observation//, not for the mean: x̄ ± t* s √(1 + 1/n). For the basket example it is 100 ± 2.064 × 15 × √1.04 = 100 ± 31.6, far wider than the interval for the mean, since individual baskets vary much more than the average does.
Always report an effect with its interval, not only a p-value: the interval shows both the size of the effect and its precision.

check.a: the procedure that produced it captures the true parameter in 95% of repeated samples
wrong: the parameter lies in this interval with probability 0.95
95% of the data lie in the interval
the sample mean is within the interval 95% of the time

check.q: Compared with a confidence interval for the mean, a prediction interval for a new observation is
check.a: wider, because it must include the variation of individual values
wrong: narrower
the same width
undefined

sections.title: The bootstrap
body: Imagine you have 100 measurements and want to know how much their average would vary if you could repeat the whole study. You cannot repeat it, but you can do the next best thing: treat your 100 measurements as a small model of the whole population, draw 100 values from them with replacement (so some values repeat and some are left out), compute the average, and repeat this thousands of times. The spread of those averages shows how much the statistic is likely to vary. To know how a statistic varies from sample to sample we would like to draw many new samples from the population, which we cannot. The **bootstrap** (Efron, 1979) uses the sample itself as a stand-in for the population: draw new samples //from the data// by resampling **with replacement**, compute the statistic on each, and use the spread of these values as the sampling distribution. This is the **plug-in principle**: the empirical distribution of the data estimates the population distribution.

list: Draw B bootstrap samples (typically B = 1000 to 10,000), each of the same size n as the data, by choosing n observations with replacement.
Compute the statistic θ̂* on each one.
The standard deviation of the θ̂* values is the **bootstrap standard error**. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the θ̂* values form a 95% **percentile interval**.

example.title: A bootstrap standard error by hand (in distribution)
example.problem: The sample is 3, 5, 7, 9, 11. What is the bootstrap standard error of the mean, and how does it compare with the usual formula?
example.solution: The mean is 7. Resampling from the data, each bootstrap observation has the data's own distribution: mean 7 and variance (1/n)Σ(x − x̄)² = 40/5 = 8. A bootstrap mean of 5 observations therefore has variance 8/5 = 1.6 and standard error √1.6 = 1.265. The usual formula s/√n uses s² = 40/4 = 10: SE = √(10/5) = 1.414. They differ by the factor √((n − 1)/n) = 0.894, a small-sample effect that vanishes as n grows. The point is that the bootstrap needs no formula: the same recipe works for any statistic.

code: return np.array([stat(x[rng.integers(0, n, size=n)]) for _ in range(B)])
boots.std()                           # bootstrap standard error of the median
np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])     # 95% percentile interval for the median
body.caption: The bootstrap for the median, a statistic with no simple formula for its standard error.

body: The same two lines of code give an interval for a trimmed mean, a ratio of means, a correlation, a regression coefficient, the area under a ROC curve or any metric of a model. Resample **rows** (or whole examples), so that the relationships between columns are preserved.

list: **Very small samples** (below about 20 to 30 for a mean, more for skewed data): the empirical distribution is a poor model of the population.
**Extreme statistics** such as the maximum or minimum: the bootstrap maximum equals the sample maximum with probability 1 − (1 − 1/n)ⁿ ≈ 63%, a degenerate distribution.

**Dependent data** (time series, clustered or grouped data): ordinary resampling breaks the dependence and understates the uncertainty. Use the **block bootstrap** (resample blocks of consecutive observations) or resample whole clusters (such as all the records of a user).
**Heavy tails and infinite variance**: the mean does not have a well-behaved sampling distribution.
**Biased samples**: the bootstrap reflects only the sampling variability, never the bias of the collection process.
The percentile interval can be inaccurate for skewed statistics; refinements such as the **BCa** (bias-corrected and accelerated) interval help.

check.a: with replacement from the observed data, with the same size as the data

from a normal distribution fitted to the data
from a random half of the data

sections.title: Precision and sample-size planning
body: Before collecting data, decide how precise the answer must be. For a mean, the half-width of the interval is w = z*·σ/√n, so the sample size needed for a target half-width is

example.title: Planning a measurement study
example.problem: Response times have σ ≈ 15 ms. How many measurements give a 95% interval for the mean with half-width 2 ms?
example.solution: n = (1.96 × 15/2)² = 14.7² = 216.1, so 217 measurements. To get the half-width down to 1 ms requires four times as many (865). A pilot study supplies the estimate of σ.

list: For a proportion use σ² = p(1 − p), with p = 0.5 as the cautious choice: n = (1.96 × 0.5/w)² (see Sampling and Experiments).

**Statistical significance is not practical significance.** With a huge sample even a trivial difference has a tiny p-value, and with a small sample an important effect may be invisible. Interpret the //size// of the effect and its interval in the units of the problem: is a 0.1% increase in conversion worth the cost of the change?

**Effect sizes** express differences in comparable units: the raw difference, a percentage change, or the standardized difference d = (x̄₁ − x̄₂)/s (Cohen's d: about 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large).
Precision costs grow as 1/w²: halving the interval width needs four times the data, and so the first improvements are cheap and the last are expensive.

check.q: To halve the width of a confidence interval for a mean you need about
wrong: twice as many
half as many
the same number with a lower confidence level

sections.title: Uncertainty for machine learning metrics
body: Test-set metrics are estimates, and the bootstrap gives them intervals without a formula for each metric.

code: idx = rng.integers(0, n, size=n)           # resample test examples
# e.g. bootstrap_metric(y, scores, roc_auc_score) gives a 95% interval for the AUC
body.caption: A bootstrap interval for any test metric: resample the test examples and recompute.

list: **Compare two models on the same test set** with a **paired** bootstrap: for each resample compute the difference between the two models' metrics (the same resampled examples for both). If the interval of the difference excludes 0, the difference is unlikely to be chance. Unpaired intervals that overlap do not mean that the models are equal: the paired comparison is much more sensitive.
Resample the **unit** that matters: for a model evaluated per patient, resample patients, not individual visits.

The interval accounts for the finite test set, not for the variation from training the model with a different seed or on different training data. Report both, by repeating training (see Randomness in Computation).

**Bagging and random forests** apply the same resampling idea to the training data: averaging models fit to bootstrap samples reduces variance (see Ensembles), and the omitted examples provide the out-of-bag error estimate.

**Cross-validation** estimates generalization error but its folds are not independent, so the naive standard error across folds is too small; the bootstrap and repeated cross-validation are alternatives.

example.title: Is the new model better?
example.problem: Model B has accuracy 0.84 and model A 0.82 on the same 500 test examples. Paired resampling gives a 95% interval of (−0.005, +0.045) for the difference B − A. What do you conclude?
example.solution: The interval includes 0, so the data are compatible with no difference or with a gain of up to 4.5 points: the two-point gain is within the noise of a test set of 500 (a single accuracy has a margin of ±3.3 points). Conclude that B may be better but the evidence is not conclusive; collect more test data, or accept B if it is also simpler or cheaper.

check.q: A paired bootstrap compares two models by
check.a: resampling the test examples and computing the difference in their metrics on each resample
wrong: training each model on bootstrap samples only
comparing the two accuracies directly
adding the two intervals

quiz.q: A sample of n = 9 has mean 40 and standard deviation s = 6. Using t* = 2.306 for 8 degrees of freedom, what is the 95% confidence interval for the mean?
quiz.why: SE = 6/√9 = 2, so the half-width is 2.306 × 2 = 4.61. The z value 1.96 would give (36.1, 43.9), too narrow for n = 9; dividing by n instead of √n gives the second option.

quiz.q: In a sample of 200 emails, 60 are flagged. What is the 95% Wald interval for the flag rate?
quiz.why: SE = √(0.3 × 0.7/200) = 0.0324, and the margin is 1.96 × 0.0324 = 0.064. One standard error is 0.032, and doubling the margin gives 0.127.

quiz.q: The same data are used to build a 99% and a 95% confidence interval for a mean. How do they compare?
quiz.a: The 99% interval is wider, since a higher level uses a larger critical value
wrong: The 99% interval is narrower, because it reflects a greater degree of certainty
They have the same width, because the standard error does not depend on the confidence level
The 99% interval is wider only when the sample size is small
quiz.why: Width is t* × SE. Capturing the parameter more often requires a larger critical value, which stretches the interval at every sample size.

quiz.q: Each of 200 independent studies builds a 95% interval for the same population mean. About how many of the intervals contain it?
wrong: All 200
About 95
About 100
quiz.why: The 95% describes the long-run success rate of the procedure, so about 0.95 × 200 = 190 intervals capture the mean and roughly 10 miss it.

quiz.q: Why does a confidence interval for a mean use a t critical value instead of 1.96 when σ is estimated by s from a small sample?
quiz.a: Estimating σ adds uncertainty, giving heavier tails and a larger multiplier
wrong: Small samples always come from skewed populations, which the t distribution corrects
The t distribution makes the interval narrower to offset the smaller sample size
The sample mean is biased for small n, and the larger t* corrects that bias exactly
quiz.why: The statistic (x̄ − μ)/(s/√n) follows a t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom. For small n, t* is larger than 1.96, and it approaches 1.96 as n grows.

quiz.q: A sample of n = 16 has mean 50 and s = 8. Using t* = 2.131, what is the half-width of the 95% prediction interval for a new observation?
wrong: About 4.3
About 8.5
About 35.1
quiz.why: The half-width is t* · s · √(1 + 1/n) = 2.131 × 8 × √1.0625 = 17.6. The 4.3 is the half-width for the mean, which ignores the variation of individual values.

quiz.q: For a large data set of n observations, about what fraction of the distinct original observations appear in a typical bootstrap sample?
wrong: About 37%
About 50%
About 95%
quiz.why: An observation is missed in all n draws with probability (1 − 1/n)ⁿ ≈ 0.37, so it appears with probability about 0.63.

quiz.q: The sample is 2, 4, 6. What is the bootstrap standard error of the mean, computed from the distribution of resampled means?
wrong: About 1.15
About 0.89
About 1.33
quiz.why: The data's own variance is (1/3)Σ(x − 4)² = 8/3, so a mean of 3 draws has variance 8/9 and standard error √(8/9) = 0.94. The usual s/√n is 1.15, and 0.89 is the variance.

quiz.q: A bootstrap produces 2000 resampled medians. Which sorted values give the 95% percentile interval?
wrong: The 25th and the 1975th
The 100th and the 1900th
The 5th and the 1995th
quiz.why: The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of 2000 values sit near positions 0.025 × 2000 = 50 and 0.975 × 2000 = 1950.

quiz.q: Why does the bootstrap perform badly for the sample maximum?
quiz.a: A bootstrap maximum equals the sample maximum about 63% of the time, so it is degenerate
wrong: The maximum is not a function of the data, so it cannot be recomputed on a resample
Bootstrap samples drawn with replacement can never contain the largest value of the data
The maximum is always normally distributed, so no resampling is required to describe it
quiz.why: Extreme statistics depend on a single observation, and resampling repeats that value in most resamples. The resulting distribution is lumpy and misrepresents the true sampling variability.

quiz.q: A bootstrap interval is computed for the mean rating in a voluntary-response online poll. What does the interval reflect?
quiz.a: Only the random sampling variability, not the bias of who chose to respond
wrong: Both sampling variability and bias, since resampling reproduces the whole collection process
The variability of the population, including the non-respondents
Nothing useful, since a bootstrap needs at least 1000 observations
quiz.why: The bootstrap treats the sample as the population, so any bias in how it was collected is copied into every resample. Intervals never account for it.

quiz.q: Response times have σ ≈ 10 ms. How many measurements give a 95% interval for the mean with half-width 1.5 ms?
quiz.why: n = (z*σ/w)² = (1.96 × 10/1.5)² = 13.07² = 170.7, rounded up to 171. Omitting the square gives 14, and dropping z* gives 45.

quiz.q: A study with n = 200 yields a 95% interval with half-width 6. About how many observations are needed to bring the half-width to 2?
quiz.why: Width is proportional to 1/√n. Dividing it by 3 needs 3² = 9 times as many observations, and 200 × 9 = 1800.

quiz.q: A test on 2 million visitors finds that conversion rose from 10.00% to 10.02%, with p = 0.001. What is the best conclusion?
quiz.a: The difference is statistically detectable but may be too small to matter
wrong: The change is large, because the p-value is very small
The change is not real, because the difference is only 0.02 points
The result is invalid, because the sample size is too large
quiz.why: With enormous samples even trivial differences give tiny p-values. Judge the size of the effect and its interval in the units of the problem.

quiz.q: Two groups have means 105 and 100 and a common standard deviation of 10. What is Cohen's d?
wrong: 5, a very large effect
0.05, a negligible effect
0.2, a small effect
quiz.why: d = (105 − 100)/10 = 0.5. The standardized difference is in units of standard deviations, and about 0.5 is conventionally called medium.

quiz.q: The 95% bootstrap intervals for the accuracies of two models on the same test set are (0.80, 0.86) and (0.82, 0.88). Can one conclude that there is no evidence of a difference?
quiz.a: No: a paired bootstrap of the difference is more sensitive and could exclude 0
wrong: Yes: overlapping intervals prove that the two models have equal accuracy
Yes: the two intervals should be added together to get the interval of the difference
No: the accuracy of one model cannot be compared with that of another model
quiz.why: Both models are scored on the same examples, so their errors are correlated and the difference has much less variability than the separate intervals suggest.

quiz.q: A bootstrap of the test examples gives an AUC interval of (0.88, 0.92). Which source of uncertainty does it leave out?
quiz.a: Variation from training the model with a different seed or on other training data
wrong: The finite size of the test set
The random choice of which test examples fall in each resample
The sampling variability of the AUC
quiz.why: Resampling the test set captures the noise from having a finite test set only. Repeating the training is needed to measure the variation caused by training itself.

quiz.q: In bagging, what do the examples omitted from a given bootstrap sample provide?
quiz.a: An out-of-bag estimate of the prediction error
wrong: A set of extra training examples for the next resample
The bootstrap standard error of the model parameters
A guarantee that the ensemble has zero bias
quiz.why: Each model is fit without the omitted examples, so predicting those examples gives an honest error estimate with no separate test set.

summary: A confidence interval for a mean is x̄ ± t*·s/√n (t with n − 1 degrees of freedom); for a proportion p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n). The 95% describes the procedure, not the probability that the parameter is in one computed interval.
Prediction intervals for a new observation are wider: x̄ ± t*·s√(1 + 1/n). Credible intervals are the Bayesian counterpart.

The bootstrap resamples the data with replacement B times, computes the statistic each time, and uses the spread (standard error) and percentiles (interval) of the results. It works for statistics with no formula, but fails for tiny samples, extremes, dependent data and bias; use block or cluster resampling for dependence.
Interval width scales as 1/√n; the sample size for half-width w is n = (z*σ/w)². Report effect sizes with intervals and judge practical significance.
Bootstrap the test examples to put intervals on model metrics, and use a paired bootstrap to compare models.

problems.q: A sample of n = 16 has x̄ = 50 and s = 8. Give a 95% t interval (t* = 2.131 for 15 degrees of freedom) and the corresponding z interval.
In a survey of 400 users, 88 clicked on a feature. Give a 95% Wald interval for the click rate.
How many observations are needed to estimate a mean with 95% half-width 0.5 when σ ≈ 4?

A bootstrap of 10,000 resamples of a median gives values with standard deviation 1.8 and 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles 31.2 and 37.9. State the bootstrap standard error and the 95% percentile interval. Why might the normal approximation (median ± 1.96 × 1.8) differ?
problems.solution: SE = 1.8; interval (31.2, 37.9). The normal approximation gives median ± 3.5. If the bootstrap distribution is asymmetric about the sample median (for example the median is 33 and the interval extends 1.8 below and 4.9 above), the percentile interval captures the skew, and the symmetric normal interval does not.
problems.a: SE 1.8; (31.2, 37.9); the percentile interval accommodates skewness.

problems.q: Why is resampling individual rows wrong when each user contributes 50 correlated rows, and what should be resampled?
problems.solution: Rows from the same user are correlated, so the effective sample size is closer to the number of users than the number of rows. Resampling rows treats them as independent and gives intervals that are too narrow. Resample whole users (a cluster bootstrap), taking all of the chosen user's rows each time.
